Which names were popular in each generation? We use published U.S. birth counts for the 14 complete decades from 1880–2019.

## Packages and helpers
```{r}
#| label: baby-preparation-setup
library(tidyverse)
source("helpers.R")
```

## Build the list of annual files
The saved files follow one naming pattern: `yob1880.txt`, `yob1881.txt`, and so on. Create the years first, then use `str_glue()` to insert each year into the filename template. For the preview, tribble() places the two sequences into list-cells. Unnest both columns together to pair each year with its path, then show the first six rows.
```{r}
#| label: list-baby-name-files
ssa_years <- 1880:2019
ssa_file_paths <- str_glue("data/raw/ssa/yob{ssa_years}.txt")

tribble(
  ~year,     ~source_file,
  ssa_years, ssa_file_paths
) |>
  unnest(c(year, source_file)) |>
  preview()
```

## Read and stack the annual files
Each file contains comma-separated name, sex and birth-count fields despite its `.txt` extension. Here `read_csv()` reads every path in the list and stacks the rows into one table. `col_names` supplies the three headings absent from the files. `id = "source_file"` adds the originating path to each row, allowing us to recover its year next. Names and sex are inferred as text; birth counts are numbers.
```{r}
#| label: read-baby-names
ssa_raw <- read_csv(
  ssa_file_paths,
  col_names = c("name", "sex", "births"),
  id = "source_file"
)

ssa_raw |>
  preview()
```

## Read the year from the filename
`str_extract()` finds the four-digit year in each source path. The pattern `[0-9]{4}` means four consecutive digits; in our paths, such as `data/raw/ssa/yob1924.txt`, those digits are the year. `as.integer()` turns the extracted text into a number.
```{r}
#| label: prepare-baby-name-years
ssa_raw |>
  mutate(year = str_extract(source_file, "[0-9]{4}")) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) ->
  ssa_with_years

ssa_with_years |>
  distinct(source_file, year) |>
  preview()
```

## Assign each year to a decade
Integer division (`%/%`) keeps the whole-number part: 1924 divided by 10 gives 192. Multiplying by 10 gives the decade label 1920. Every year from 1920 through 1929 receives that label. Keep the prepared year and remove the source path from this working table.
```{r}
#| label: prepare-baby-name-decades
ssa_with_years |>
  mutate(decade = (year %/% 10) * 10) |>
  select(name, sex, year, decade, births) ->
  ssa_with_decades

# Show a decade boundary and the ends of the selected period.
ssa_with_decades |>
  distinct(year, decade) |>
  filter(year %in% c(1880, 1889, 1890, 2019))
```

## Give names the same matching format as the dogs
Uppercase the names, then remove spaces and hyphens using the same two steps as dog preparation. Keep each full name rather than splitting it into words.
```{r}
#| label: format-baby-names
ssa_with_decades |>
  mutate(name = str_to_upper(name)) |>
  mutate(name = str_remove_all(name, "[\\s-]")) ->
  baby_names_yearly_prepared

# Display the same formatting operations on six distinct recorded names.
ssa_with_decades |>
  distinct(name) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  rename(recorded_name = name) |>
  mutate(name = str_to_upper(recorded_name)) |>
  mutate(name = str_remove_all(name, "[\\s-]"))
```

## Total births by name and decade
Add the published birth counts across all years and both sex categories. These counts cover the births represented in the SSA files, with the suppression and historical coverage limits described below.
```{r}
#| label: count-baby-names
baby_names_yearly_prepared |>
  group_by(name, decade) |>
  summarise(births = sum(births)) |>
  ungroup() ->
  ssa_decade_counts

ssa_decade_counts |>
  preview()
```

## Rank names within each decade
Within each decade, put the largest birth counts first, breaking ties alphabetically. `.by_group = TRUE` keeps each decade together while sorting. `row_number()` numbers the sorted names starting at 1 for each decade. Keep the full ranked table for inspection; the next step selects ranks 1 through 100. The final display shows the first five names per decade.
```{r}
#| label: rank-baby-names
ssa_decade_counts |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  arrange(desc(births), name, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() ->
  baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared

baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared |>
  filter(rank <= 5)
```

## Keep the top 100 names for each decade
Keep rows with a rank of 100 or less, then keep just the decade and name. This gives 100 names for each of the 14 decades: 1,400 rows in all. A name can appear in more than one decade's list.
```{r}
#| label: select-top-100-names
baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared |>
  filter(rank <= 100) |>
  select(decade, name) ->
  baby_names_top100_by_decade_prepared

# Show three names from each of three decades; the prepared table retains all fourteen.
baby_names_top100_by_decade_prepared |>
  filter(decade %in% c(1880, 1950, 2010)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  ungroup()
```

### See which decades enter the top 100
Use ALICE and OLIVER as consistent examples in all four charts. The gray line shows each name's recorded births; blue circles mark decades selected by the top-100 rule. A decade can qualify even when it is far from that name's own peak. Each panel has its own birth-count scale so both histories are readable; compare timing rather than line heights between names.
```{r}
#| label: visualize-top100-name-decades
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
name_measure_examples <- c("ALICE", "OLIVER")

baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared |>
  filter(name %in% name_measure_examples) ->
  example_name_decades

example_name_decades |>
  filter(rank <= 100) ->
  example_top100_decades

example_name_decades |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = births)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray55") +
  geom_point(data = example_top100_decades, color = "#0072B2", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  labs(title = "1. Top-100 decades", subtitle = "Blue circles: rank 100 or better", x = "Decade starting", y = "Recorded births in decade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ->
  top100_decades_plot

top100_decades_plot
```

## Find each name's peak birth-count decade
For each name, keep the decade with the largest published birth count. `with_ties = TRUE` retains every decade sharing that maximum. These references cover all recorded names, not only top-100 names.
```{r}
#| label: baby-name-peak-count-decade
baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared |>
  group_by(name) |>
  slice_max(order_by = births, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    name,
    peak_birth_count_decade = decade,
    peak_birth_count = births
  ) ->
  baby_names_peak_birth_count_decade

baby_names_peak_birth_count_decade |>
  preview()
```

### See the peak birth-count decades
Keep the same birth-count curves, but now highlight the selected maximum rather than top-100 membership. Orange diamonds show every tied peak if there is more than one.
```{r}
#| label: visualize-peak-count-name-decades
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
baby_names_peak_birth_count_decade |>
  filter(name %in% name_measure_examples) ->
  example_peak_decades

example_name_decades |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = births)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray55") +
  geom_point(data = example_peak_decades,
             aes(x = peak_birth_count_decade, y = peak_birth_count),
             color = "#D55E00", shape = 18, size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  labs(title = "2. Peak birth-count decades", subtitle = "Orange diamonds: largest birth count for this name", x = "Decade starting", y = "Recorded births in decade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ->
  peak_count_decades_plot

peak_count_decades_plot
```

## Find each name's highest-ranked decade
A smaller rank means a higher position. Keep the smallest rank each name achieved, retaining all decades with that same rank. This uses the existing ranking, which breaks equal birth counts alphabetically within a decade. Peak count and highest rank can differ: the decade with the most births bearing a name need not be the decade when it ranked highest against other names.
```{r}
#| label: baby-name-best-rank-decade
baby_names_rank_by_decade_prepared |>
  group_by(name) |>
  slice_min(order_by = rank, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(name, decade, rank) ->
  baby_names_best_rank_decade

baby_names_best_rank_decade |>
  preview()
```

### See the highest-ranked decades
This chart changes the vertical axis to rank: smaller numbers indicate a higher rank and appear higher on the chart. Green squares mark the name's highest position against other names, retaining ties. The dashed line marks rank 100. The highest rank does not necessarily occur at the name's largest birth count.
```{r}
#| label: visualize-best-rank-name-decades
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
baby_names_best_rank_decade |>
  filter(name %in% name_measure_examples) ->
  example_best_rank_decades

example_name_decades |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = rank)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray55") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray65") +
  geom_point(data = example_best_rank_decades, color = "#007F5F", shape = 15, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~name) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  labs(title = "3. Highest-ranked decades", subtitle = "Green squares: smallest rank; higher on chart means better", x = "Decade starting", y = "Rank among names") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ->
  best_rank_decades_plot

best_rank_decades_plot
```

### Put name counts in context
The overall number of births represented in the files changes over time. A larger name count can reflect a larger birth cohort as well as a change in naming preferences. The chart below shows each name’s percentage of recorded births. The average-year illustrations below overlay total births and name counts, using separately labeled vertical axes. These totals cover published SSA records, not the population alive that year or a complete count of all births; historical coverage and suppressed small counts affect the denominator.

First total the published birth counts across every name and both sex categories for each year.
```{r}
#| label: total-recorded-births-by-year
baby_names_yearly_prepared |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(recorded_births_in_year = sum(births)) |>
  ungroup() ->
  recorded_birth_totals_by_year

recorded_birth_totals_by_year |>
  preview()
```

For the two example names, combine the sex categories within each year. These same annual name counts also supply the average-year illustrations below.
```{r}
#| label: prepare-example-annual-name-counts
baby_names_yearly_prepared |>
  filter(name %in% name_measure_examples) |>
  group_by(name, year) |>
  summarise(births = sum(births)) |>
  ungroup() ->
  example_name_years

example_name_years |>
  preview()
```

Attach the year's total to each example name's count. The left join matches by year; there is one denominator row per year. Dividing the name count by that total gives its share. These shares are for explaining the measures, not a new column in the dog table or a replacement for the decade ranks.
```{r}
#| label: calculate-example-name-shares
example_name_years |>
  left_join(recorded_birth_totals_by_year, by = "year") |>
  mutate(share_of_recorded_births = births / recorded_births_in_year) ->
  example_name_birth_shares

example_name_birth_shares |>
  preview()
```

```{r}
#| label: build-name-share-plot
example_name_birth_shares |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = share_of_recorded_births)) +
  geom_line(color = "#007F5F", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Share of recorded births", subtitle = "Name count ÷ all recorded births that year", x = "Birth year", y = "Percentage with this name") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ->
  example_name_birth_shares_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: show-name-shares
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
example_name_birth_shares_plot
```

A share measures the fraction of recorded births receiving the name. A rank measures its position against other names. Those are different comparisons, and the year of highest share need not match the year of highest count or the highest-ranked decade. The early years also have less complete SSA coverage, so interpret their shares in that context.

## Weight each birth year by its recorded birth count
Multiply each year by the number of births recorded for that name and sex. For example, 10 births in 1950 contribute 19,500 to the total. A year with more births contributes more to the eventual average.
```{r}
#| label: weight-baby-name-years
baby_names_yearly_prepared |>
  mutate(birth_year_total = year * births) ->
  baby_names_weighted_years

baby_names_weighted_years |>
  select(name, year, births, birth_year_total) |>
  preview()
```

## Total the weighted years for each name
Add the weighted years and birth counts across all selected years and both sex categories.
```{r}
#| label: total-weighted-baby-name-years
baby_names_weighted_years |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(
    birth_year_total = sum(birth_year_total),
    total_births = sum(births)
  ) |>
  ungroup() ->
  baby_names_year_totals

baby_names_year_totals |>
  preview()
```

## Calculate each name's weighted average birth year
Divide the weighted-year total by the birth count. The result is the average birth year among the published records bearing that name in 1880–2019. It is not the average age of people alive today or necessarily a popularity peak: two separated periods of popularity can place the average between them. Keep fractional years rather than rounding the reference values.
```{r}
#| label: average-baby-name-birth-year
baby_names_year_totals |>
  mutate(average_birth_year = birth_year_total / total_births) |>
  select(name, average_birth_year) ->
  baby_names_average_birth_year

baby_names_average_birth_year |>
  preview()
```

### See the weighted average for ALICE and OLIVER
The gray area shows the name’s annual birth count on the left axis. The blue line shows all recorded SSA births on the blue right axis, repeated in both name panels. Both counts combine the sex categories. For display only, total births are divided by 300; the right axis multiplies those positions back by 300. This same conversion and fixed limits apply throughout the comparison. Line crossings do not mean equal counts. The share chart above shows the actual name-to-total proportion. The purple dashed line marks the weighted average year, with its value rounded only for the display. It summarizes the whole selected history rather than choosing a peak; it can sit in a quieter period between waves of popularity. The horizontal axis here is an individual year, not a decade label.
```{r}
#| label: visualize-average-name-year
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
# One fixed display conversion for both names and both average charts.
total_births_axis_multiplier <- 300

recorded_birth_totals_by_year |>
  mutate(total_births_plot_height = recorded_births_in_year / total_births_axis_multiplier) ->
  total_births_overlay

baby_names_average_birth_year |>
  filter(name %in% name_measure_examples) |>
  mutate(display_average_year = round(average_birth_year, 1)) |>
  mutate(average_label = str_glue("Weighted mean: {display_average_year}")) ->
  example_average_years

example_name_years |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = births)) +
  geom_area(fill = "gray80") +
  geom_line(color = "gray55") +
  geom_line(data = total_births_overlay,
            aes(x = year, y = total_births_plot_height), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(data = example_average_years,
             aes(xintercept = average_birth_year), color = "#8451A1", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = example_average_years,
            aes(x = average_birth_year, y = Inf, label = average_label),
            color = "#8451A1", vjust = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~name) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 16000), breaks = c(0, 5000, 10000, 15000),
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * total_births_axis_multiplier,
                        name = "All recorded SSA births (blue)", labels = scales::label_comma())
  ) +
  labs(title = "4. Weighted average baby birth year", subtitle = "Purple line: average weighted by recorded births", x = "Birth year", y = "Births with this name (gray)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
        axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
        axis.ticks.y.right = element_line(color = "#0072B2")) ->
  average_birth_year_plot

average_birth_year_plot
```

### Compare unweighted and weighted averages for ALICE and OLIVER
For this explanatory comparison only, give each distinct recorded year equal weight. Annual counts have already been combined across sex, so a year is counted once. This ignores how many babies received the name that year. The weighted panel uses those counts. Read across each name: both panels show the same annual birth-count curve with matching axes, but the average markers differ. Years with more births contribute more to the weighted average; every recorded year contributes equally to the unweighted average. If a name appears in all 140 years, its unweighted mean is simply the midpoint of 1880–2019, regardless of its popularity pattern. This unweighted measure is not added to the dog table.
```{r}
#| label: build-unweighted-name-year-comparison
example_name_years |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(unweighted_average_year = mean(year)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(display_average_year = round(unweighted_average_year, 1)) |>
  mutate(average_label = str_glue("Unweighted mean: {display_average_year}")) ->
  example_unweighted_years

example_name_years |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = births)) +
  geom_area(fill = "gray80") +
  geom_line(color = "gray55") +
  geom_line(data = total_births_overlay,
            aes(x = year, y = total_births_plot_height), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(data = example_unweighted_years,
             aes(xintercept = unweighted_average_year), color = "#D55E00", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = example_unweighted_years,
            aes(x = unweighted_average_year, y = Inf, label = average_label),
            color = "#D55E00", vjust = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~name) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 16000), breaks = c(0, 5000, 10000, 15000),
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * total_births_axis_multiplier,
                        name = "All recorded SSA births (blue)", labels = scales::label_comma())
  ) +
  labs(title = "Unweighted average year", subtitle = "Orange line: each distinct recorded year counts equally", x = "Birth year", y = "Births with this name (gray)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
        axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
        axis.ticks.y.right = element_line(color = "#0072B2")) ->
  unweighted_birth_year_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-average-name-years
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
unweighted_birth_year_plot +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1)
average_birth_year_plot +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1)
```

### Compare the four measures together
These are the same four charts shown beside the calculations, reused without recalculating the references. Read them as four different questions: when was the name in the top 100; when did it have the most births; when did it rank highest; and where is the weighted center of its recorded birth years? The first two use decade birth counts, the third uses rank, and the fourth uses annual birth counts. The heights are not interchangeable across these measures. These examples explain the measures; they are not evidence of an income relationship.
```{r}
#| label: compare-name-measure-plots
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
top100_decades_plot
peak_count_decades_plot
best_rank_decades_plot
average_birth_year_plot
```

## Make a list of all recorded SSA names
Use the formatted annual records so this table includes names outside the top 100. `distinct(name)` keeps one column, with each name appearing once. This is the reference for names appearing anywhere in the selected 1880–2019 SSA records.
```{r}
#| label: list-all-ssa-names
baby_names_yearly_prepared |>
  distinct(name) ->
  all_distinct_baby_names

all_distinct_baby_names |>
  preview()
```

SSA omits names reported fewer than five times for a sex and year. Early birth years have less complete coverage because many people born before 1937 never applied for a Social Security card. These limits affect the historical comparisons.
